newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Police to tighten security for Australian race MP.
newsitem.headline: Police to tighten security for Australian race MP.

text.p: Australian police said on Tuesday they would tighten up security at a country rally to be attended by race row politician Pauline Hanson after several people were injured during anti-Hanson protests on Monday.

Police said a small group of activists were responsible for the violence at the launch of Hanson's One Nation party in the Victorian rural town of Dandenong, where protesters threw potatoes, eggs and urine-filled balloons.
Those injured included a 60-year-old Hanson supporter attacked by protesters. The man spent the night in hospital.
A former Australian deputy prime minister, 82-year-old Jim Cairns, joined in the protests but was thrown out of the meeting after he started distributing anti-Hanson tracts.
Queenslander Hanson is due next week to attend a rally in the Victorian town of Geelong and another counter-demonstration is being organised.
"We're taking certain precautions," said acting Chief Superintendent Alan MacLean of the Geelong police. "I will have sufficient police there on the evening to maintain the community peace."
Up to 1,500 protesters disrupted the One Nation meeting in Dandenong on Monday night. The party launch was attended by 150 Hanson supporters but not by Hanson herself.
Police Superintendent Jim Hart said he had no doubt that militant minorities, rather then genuine demonstrators, were responsible for the violence.

"A large number of those demonstrating are genuine people wishing to voice their concerns," Hart said. "There are other groups, however, that infiltrate and they are the ones that cause the problems."
Police said they were studying videos of the meeting to identify the protesters who attacked the 60-year-old man. Seven arrests had already been made and more could follow.
One Nation spokesman David Ettridge said the protest was the worst he had ever seen at a Hanson rally -- other One Nation regional launches over the past three months have attracted noisy protests.

But Cairns, deputy prime minister under Labor's Gough Whitlam in the 1970s, said the protesters had not been violent. Cairns said One Nation's private security "muscle men" had bundled him from the meeting.

One Nation, which has an anti-immigration platform and also campaigns against Aboriginal welfare, has attracted support away from Australia's main political parties to become the country's third political force.

An opinion poll published on Tuesday showed six-percent support for the independent politician and her party, which was only officially registered last month. Hanson is the only elected member of her party and it has yet to be tested at an election.
